name: Security operations
description: Identity, secrets, threat modelling, incident response.

cards.subject: Authentication
says: verifies that a requester is who they claim to be
checks a claimed identity against proof such as a password or key
cards.use: need to confirm who is signing in
not: decides which records a signed-in user may open

cards.subject: Authorisation
says: decides what an authenticated identity is allowed to do
must be checked on the server for every request
cards.use: need to decide whether a signed-in user may open a particular record
not: proves that the person is who they say they are

cards.subject: Least privilege
says: grants only the access needed to do the task
limits the damage a compromised account can cause
cards.use: give a new starter access to systems
not: gives every employee administrator rights to avoid support requests

cards.subject: Role-based access control
says: grants permissions through roles rather than to individuals
lets many people with the same job share an identical access set
cards.use: have many staff with the same job who need identical access
not: assigns every permission directly to each person

cards.subject: Separation of duties
says: splits a sensitive process so no single person can complete it alone
stops one person both raising and approving the same payment
cards.use: need to stop one person from both requesting and approving a change
not: gives one trusted administrator control of the whole process

cards.subject: Service account
says: is an identity used by software rather than by a person
should hold its own narrowly scoped permissions
cards.use: need an application to call another system without a person signing in
not: should share the administrator's own password

cards.subject: Privileged access management
says: controls and records the use of administrator-level accounts
can issue elevated rights that expire after use
cards.use: need a record of who used administrator rights and why
not: removes the need to review privileged accounts

cards.subject: Just-in-time access
says: grants elevated rights only for a limited window after a request
leaves no standing administrator rights between tasks
cards.use: want administrators to hold no permanent elevated rights
not: gives a permanent administrator role to anyone who asks once

cards.subject: Break-glass account
says: is an emergency administrator account kept sealed for use when normal access fails
triggers an alert whenever it is used
cards.use: must regain control when the identity provider is down
not: is used every day by the administration team

cards.subject: Zero trust
says: treats network location as no proof of trustworthiness
verifies each request using identity, device state and context
cards.use: want access decisions that do not assume the office network is safe
not: trusts any request that arrives from inside the corporate network

cards.subject: Multi-factor authentication
says: requires proof from two or more different categories of factor
keeps a stolen password alone from opening the account
cards.use: want a stolen password on its own to be useless
not: is satisfied by entering two different passwords

cards.subject: Single sign-on
says: lets one login at an identity provider open many applications
gives a single place to disable a leaver's access to connected apps
cards.use: want one place to cut a leaver's access to every connected application
not: makes every application store its own copy of each password

cards.subject: Password manager
says: generates and stores a unique password for each account
fills credentials only on the site they were saved for
cards.use: need a different strong password for every account
not: is best used by reusing one strong master password on all sites

cards.subject: Password hashing
says: stores a one-way, deliberately slow transformation of the password
lets a server check a password without keeping it
cards.use: must store user passwords in a database
not: encrypts passwords so support staff can read them back

cards.subject: Passkey
says: signs in with a public-key credential bound to the site's domain
does not work on a look-alike domain, which blunts phishing
cards.use: want sign-in that a fake login page cannot capture
not: sends a reusable shared secret to the server at each sign-in

cards.subject: Authenticator app
says: generates time-based one-time codes from a secret held on the device
works without a phone signal
cards.use: want a second factor that does not rely on the phone network
not: is phishing-resistant because the code cannot be typed into a fake page

cards.subject: SMS one-time code
says: delivers a code over the phone network
is exposed to SIM-swap fraud
cards.use: hear that an attacker has persuaded a carrier to move a victim's number
not: is stronger than a hardware key because phones are always at hand

cards.subject: Hardware security key
says: answers a cryptographic challenge tied to the site's origin
gives phishing-resistant second-factor sign-in
cards.use: want a second factor that a phishing page cannot relay
not: generates codes that a user types in, so a fake page can still capture them

cards.subject: OAuth 2.0
says: lets an app obtain limited access to a resource through tokens without the user's password
issues access tokens with scopes
cards.use: need a third-party app to read part of a user's data without handing over the password
not: is a password hashing scheme

cards.subject: OpenID Connect
says: adds an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0
returns an ID token describing who signed in
cards.use: need an app to learn who the user is, not just obtain access to data
not: replaces TLS between browser and server

cards.subject: Secrets scanning
says: searches commits and files for credential patterns
can block a push that contains a key
cards.use: want to catch API keys before they reach a shared repository
not: encrypts the secrets it finds so they are safe

cards.subject: Secret rotation
says: replaces a credential so the old value stops working
is the first fix once a key has been exposed
cards.use: learn that a key was pasted into a team chat
not: can be skipped if the message is deleted quickly

cards.subject: Separate secrets per environment
says: stops a leak in staging from unlocking production
gives each environment its own keys
cards.use: worry that a test server leak could open the live system
not: reuses the production key everywhere for convenience

cards.subject: Least-privilege API key
says: carries only the permissions the integration needs
limits what a thief can do with a leaked key
cards.use: create a key for a service that only sends email
not: is simpler to manage when it has full account access

cards.subject: A secret committed to Git
says: stays readable in history after a later commit deletes the file
must be treated as compromised and rotated
cards.use: find a key in an old commit of a repository
not: is made safe by deleting the file in the next commit

cards.subject: Secrets manager
says: stores secrets centrally with access control and audit logs
can rotate credentials automatically
cards.use: have many services that each need credentials and want a record of who read them
not: keeps secrets in a plain file next to the code

cards.subject: Failing closed
says: refuses to operate when a required protection is missing
prefers an outage over silently dropping a safeguard
cards.use: decide what a service does when its encryption key is missing
not: falls back to plaintext so users notice nothing

cards.subject: Log redaction
says: removes credential values before output is written
keeps tokens and passwords out of log files
cards.use: worry that request logs record authorisation headers
not: records full request headers to make debugging easier

cards.subject: A short-lived credential
says: expires automatically after minutes or hours
reduces the value of a stolen token
cards.use: want a stolen token to stop working soon without anyone acting
not: are valid until someone remembers to revoke them

cards.subject: Envelope encryption
says: encrypts data with a data key that is itself encrypted by a master key
lets the master key change without re-encrypting all the data
cards.use: need to rotate a master key without re-encrypting every record
not: encrypts each file twice with the same key

cards.subject: Full-disk encryption
says: protects the data on a lost or stolen laptop
makes the drive unreadable without the key or credential
cards.use: worry about a laptop left on a train
not: stops malware from running on the device

cards.subject: Screen lock
says: requires a credential after a short idle period
stops a passer-by using an unattended session
cards.use: leave your desk for a few minutes
not: is only needed on devices used outside the office

cards.subject: Mobile device management
says: enforces settings on enrolled devices
can remotely wipe a lost phone
cards.use: must apply a security baseline and wipe lost phones centrally
not: is a form of password hashing

cards.subject: Removing local administrator rights
says: stops everyday accounts installing arbitrary software
limits what malware can change on a device
cards.use: want malware run by a user to have less power on the machine
not: makes the user's laptop impossible to update

cards.subject: System hardening
says: removes unnecessary services and accounts
sets secure defaults before a system goes live
cards.use: are about to put a new server into service
not: adds extra software to the server to make it harder to use

cards.subject: Device compliance check
says: grants access to apps only when the device meets a baseline
tests that the disk is encrypted and the system is patched
cards.use: want to block sign-ins from laptops that are unpatched
not: checks the user's identity and ignores the device

cards.subject: Endpoint detection and response
says: records process-level activity on devices
lets responders isolate a host remotely
cards.use: need to see what a suspicious process did and cut that laptop off the network
not: only compares files against a list of known signatures

cards.subject: Application allowlisting
says: runs only software that has been approved
blocks unknown programs by default
cards.use: want everything not explicitly approved to be refused on a device
not: blocks only the programs on a list of known malware

cards.subject: Vulnerability
says: is a weakness that could be exploited
may exist in code, configuration or process
cards.use: hear that a flaw could let an attacker in
not: is the same thing as an attack in progress

cards.subject: Patch management
says: tracks, tests and applies software updates
closes known vulnerabilities in a planned way
cards.use: need a routine for rolling out vendor fixes
not: means installing updates only after an incident

cards.subject: CVE identifier
says: gives a public unique name to a disclosed vulnerability
lets different tools refer to the same flaw
cards.use: need a common reference for a specific disclosed vulnerability across scanners and advisories
not: scores how severe the flaw is for your environment

cards.subject: Vulnerability scan
says: automatically checks systems for known weaknesses
produces a list of findings to triage
cards.use: want a regular automated sweep for known weaknesses
not: proves a flaw can be exploited by actually breaking in

cards.subject: CVSS score
says: rates the technical severity of a vulnerability from 0 to 10
does not know how exposed your own systems are
cards.use: need a standard severity number for a flaw
not: measures how likely your company is to be targeted

cards.subject: Penetration test
says: has authorised testers try to exploit weaknesses
shows real-world impact rather than a list of possibilities
cards.use: want to know whether an attacker could chain weaknesses to reach sensitive data
not: is carried out without the owner's permission

cards.subject: Zero-day
says: is a vulnerability exploited before a patch exists
gives defenders no fix to apply on the day of attack
cards.use: hear of an exploited flaw for which the vendor has no fix yet
not: is a flaw that has been patched for a long time

cards.subject: Dependency scanning
says: flags known-vulnerable libraries used by a project
reads the manifest or lock file
cards.use: want to know whether any library your app uses has a published flaw
not: tests your own source code for logic errors

cards.subject: Risk-based prioritisation
says: ranks fixes by exploitability, exposure and asset value
can put an internet-facing flaw ahead of a higher-scored internal one
cards.use: have hundreds of findings and must choose what to fix first
not: fixes findings in strict order of their CVSS score

cards.subject: Compensating control
says: reduces risk when a fix cannot be applied yet
might isolate a system that cannot be patched
cards.use: cannot patch a legacy system this month
not: is a way of formally deleting the vulnerability from the register

cards.subject: An audit log
says: records who did what and when
should be protected from alteration by the people it records
cards.use: need to show who changed a permission last week
not: is a performance trace meant only for debugging

cards.subject: A SIEM
says: collects and correlates logs from many sources
raises alerts when events match detection rules
cards.use: want events from servers, identity and cloud tools in one searchable place with alerts
not: is a firewall that blocks traffic itself

cards.subject: Alert fatigue
says: builds up when too many low-value alerts bury real ones
leads analysts to ignore or silence alerts
cards.use: notice analysts closing alerts without reading them
not: is solved by adding more alert rules of every kind

cards.subject: A behavioural baseline
says: describes what normal activity looks like
lets unusual behaviour stand out
cards.use: want to spot a user downloading far more data than usual
not: is a list of known malicious file hashes

cards.subject: An indicator of compromise
says: is an observable artefact such as a malicious domain or file hash
can be searched for across logs after a report
cards.use: receive a threat report listing malicious domains and need to check whether you saw them
not: describes what normal activity looks like

cards.subject: Off-host log forwarding
says: copies logs to a separate store as they are written
keeps an intruder from erasing the evidence on the compromised host
cards.use: fear an intruder will delete the local logs on a server they control
not: is needed only when disk space runs out

cards.subject: A correlation rule
says: combines several events into one detection
might fire on many failed sign-ins followed by a success
cards.use: want to detect many failed logins followed by a success from one address
not: alerts on any single login event

cards.subject: A canary token
says: is a decoy credential or file with no legitimate use
alerts whenever it is touched
cards.use: want a near-certain signal that someone is snooping where they should not
not: generates a daily report of normal activity

cards.subject: Preparation
says: puts plans, contacts and tooling in place before an incident
includes knowing who to call and where logs are
cards.use: want to be ready before anything goes wrong
not: begins after the incident is declared

cards.subject: Detection and analysis
says: confirms whether an event is a real incident
works out its scope and affected systems
cards.use: see an alert and must decide whether it is real and how big
not: removes the attacker's access

cards.subject: Containment
says: limits the spread of an incident
may isolate a host or disable an account while preserving evidence
cards.use: must stop an attacker spreading before anything is cleaned up
not: rebuilds systems from known-good images

cards.subject: Eradication
says: removes the cause, such as malware or a persistence mechanism
closes the hole the attacker used
cards.use: have contained an incident and must now remove the attacker's foothold
not: restores normal service for users

cards.subject: Recovery
says: restores service from a known-good state
is followed by closer monitoring for a repeat
cards.use: need to bring systems back after the cause has been removed
not: limits the spread of an attack in progress

cards.subject: A post-incident review
says: writes down a timeline, root cause and follow-up actions
is blameless about the people involved
cards.use: want to learn from an incident once it is over
not: is held only to decide whom to discipline

cards.subject: Chain of custody
says: documents who handled evidence and when
keeps evidence reliable if it is later challenged
cards.use: may need evidence to stand up to later scrutiny
not: is the order in which servers are rebuilt

cards.subject: Incident severity classification
says: classifies an incident by impact
decides response urgency and who must be told
cards.use: must decide whether to wake the on-call team and notify executives
not: ranks vulnerabilities by their CVSS number

cards.subject: A runbook
says: is a step-by-step procedure written in advance for a known event type
reduces improvisation under pressure
cards.use: want responders to follow agreed steps for a recurring type of alert
not: is a record of what actually happened after an incident

cards.subject: A tabletop exercise
says: walks the team through a simulated incident in discussion
exposes gaps in plans without touching live systems
cards.use: want to test the incident plan without disrupting systems
not: attacks production systems to find weaknesses

cards.subject: Breach notification duty
says: may oblige you to inform regulators or affected people
runs to deadlines set by the applicable law
cards.use: suspect personal data was taken and must decide who has to be told
not: applies only when the company chooses to announce it

cards.subject: Phishing
says: sends mass messages impersonating a trusted sender
aims to steal credentials or run malware
cards.use: get an unexpected email asking you to sign in through a link
not: is a phone call to a named individual

cards.subject: Spear phishing
says: targets one person using personal or role details
is more convincing than a mass message
cards.use: get a message that uses your manager's name and a real project
not: is sent unchanged to millions of random addresses

cards.subject: Vishing
says: uses a phone call to extract information or actions
often impersonates a help desk or bank
cards.use: get a call from someone claiming to be IT who asks for your code
not: delivers the lure by text message

cards.subject: Business email compromise
says: impersonates an executive or supplier to redirect a payment
often needs no malware at all
cards.use: get an urgent request from the apparent director to change supplier bank details
not: encrypts files and demands payment for the key

cards.subject: Brute force
says: tries many guesses against one account
is slowed by lockouts and rate limiting
cards.use: see thousands of password guesses against a single account
not: tries one common password across many accounts

cards.subject: Password spraying
says: tries a few common passwords across many accounts
stays under per-account lockout thresholds
cards.use: see one common password tried once against every account
not: replays username and password pairs leaked from another site

cards.subject: Credential stuffing
says: replays username and password pairs leaked from other sites
succeeds where people reuse passwords
cards.use: see logins succeed using real credentials from an old breach elsewhere
not: guesses passwords from a short list across every account

cards.subject: MFA fatigue
says: floods a user with approval prompts until one is accepted
is blunted by number matching and rate limits on prompts
cards.use: see a user receive dozens of push approvals at night
not: steals a code by relaying the sign-in page

cards.subject: Adversary-in-the-middle phishing
says: proxies the real sign-in page to capture the session after MFA
is defeated by phishing-resistant credentials such as passkeys
cards.use: see a stolen session cookie used after the user had completed MFA
not: only works when the victim has no second factor

cards.subject: Ransomware
says: encrypts data and demands payment for the key
often deletes or encrypts backups it can reach
cards.use: find files renamed and a note demanding payment
not: silently copies data without altering it

cards.subject: The 3-2-1 backup rule
says: keeps three copies on two kinds of media with one offsite
survives the loss of any single copy or site
cards.use: need a simple standard for how many backup copies to keep
not: keeps one copy on one disk and checks it each year

cards.subject: A restore test
says: proves a backup can actually be restored
reveals how long recovery really takes
cards.use: want evidence that backups are usable and not just present
not: checks that the backup job reported success

cards.subject: An immutable backup
says: cannot be altered or deleted during its retention period
withstands an attacker who has administrator credentials
cards.use: fear ransomware will delete backups using stolen admin rights
not: can be edited by any administrator at any time

cards.subject: An offline backup
says: is kept disconnected so ransomware cannot reach it
relies on physical or logical separation from the network
cards.use: want a copy that is unreachable from the network
not: stays mounted on the server for speed

cards.subject: Recovery point objective
says: states how much data loss, measured in time, is tolerable
sets how often backups must run
cards.use: must decide how many hours of data the business can afford to lose
not: states how long the service may be down

cards.subject: Recovery time objective
says: states how long a service may be down
drives the choice of recovery method
cards.use: must decide how fast a service has to be back
not: states how much data may be lost

cards.subject: A disaster recovery plan
says: describes how IT systems and data are restored after a major failure
assigns roles and an order of restoration
cards.use: need documented steps to rebuild systems after losing a site
not: covers only how staff keep working without computers

cards.subject: A firewall
says: filters traffic by rules on addresses, ports and protocols
denies what no rule allows
cards.use: want only certain ports reachable from the internet
not: inspects the meaning of every web request for attack patterns

cards.subject: Network segmentation
says: divides a network into zones
limits how far a breach can spread
cards.use: want a compromised laptop unable to reach the database servers
not: merges every system onto one flat network

cards.subject: A VPN
says: creates an encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network
extends a private network to remote users
cards.use: need remote staff to reach internal systems over the internet
not: splits one network into isolated zones

cards.subject: TLS
says: encrypts data in transit
authenticates the server using a certificate
cards.use: want traffic between browser and server unreadable on the way
not: encrypts data stored on the server's disk

cards.subject: A web application firewall
says: filters HTTP requests for attack patterns
can block injection attempts before they reach the app
cards.use: want a filter in front of a website that recognises injection attempts
not: only allows or denies ports and addresses

cards.subject: Defence in depth
says: layers several independent controls
means one control failing does not expose everything
cards.use: want protection that survives a single control failing
not: relies on one very strong perimeter control

cards.subject: Shared responsibility model
says: makes the cloud provider responsible for the underlying infrastructure
leaves configuration, data and identities with the customer
cards.use: wonder who must secure the settings of a storage bucket in the cloud
not: hands all security duties to the provider once you sign up

cards.subject: Cloud misconfiguration
says: exposes data when a bucket or database is left open
is a customer-side error rather than a provider flaw
cards.use: find that a storage bucket is readable by anyone on the internet
not: is caused by a flaw in the provider's hypervisor

cards.subject: Cloud security posture management
says: continuously checks cloud settings against a baseline
flags drift such as a newly public bucket
cards.use: want an automatic alert when someone makes a cloud resource public
not: encrypts data held in cloud storage

cards.subject: Egress filtering
says: restricts outbound connections
stops a compromised host reaching attacker servers
cards.use: want a compromised server unable to call out to an attacker's host
not: blocks only inbound connections

cards.subject: Lateral movement
says: is an attacker's step from one system to others after a foothold
is hampered by segmentation and unique credentials
cards.use: see a compromised workstation connecting to many internal servers
not: is the first step of gaining entry from the internet

cards.subject: An access review
says: has owners periodically confirm who still needs access
removes access that is no longer justified
cards.use: want to find leavers and role-changers who still have access
not: tests applications for software flaws

cards.subject: Security awareness training
says: teaches staff to spot and report threats
works best when reporting is easy and blame-free
cards.use: want staff to recognise phishing and know how to report it
not: replaces technical controls

cards.subject: A phishing simulation
says: sends harmless fake phishing messages
measures reporting and gives targeted coaching
cards.use: want to measure how staff react to phishing without real risk
not: is a tool for punishing people who click

cards.subject: A vendor risk assessment
says: evaluates a supplier's security before and during the relationship
looks at what data and access the supplier will have
cards.use: are about to give a new supplier access to customer data
not: is done only once on the day the contract is signed

cards.subject: A SOC 2 report
says: is an independent auditor's report on a service provider's controls
covers a period in its Type II form
cards.use: ask a supplier for independent assurance over how its controls operated
not: certifies that the supplier can never be breached

cards.subject: ISO 27001
says: is a standard for an information security management system
requires continual improvement and management review
cards.use: want a recognised standard for running an information security management system
not: is a technical specification for encryption algorithms

cards.subject: Audit evidence
says: shows that a control actually operated
can be logs, tickets, approvals or screenshots with dates
cards.use: are asked by an auditor to prove access reviews took place
not: is a verbal assurance from the control owner

cards.subject: Risk acceptance
says: is a documented decision to live with a risk
is made by the accountable owner, not by the security team alone
cards.use: decide not to fix a low-impact finding and must record it properly
not: means the risk is ignored and unrecorded

cards.subject: Data minimisation
says: collects and keeps only the data needed
shrinks what a breach can expose
cards.use: want to reduce what could leak if a system is breached
not: keeps all data in case it is useful later

cards.subject: A threat model
says: identifies assets, attackers and trust boundaries
is done before attackers get the chance
cards.use: are designing a feature and want to find security problems early
not: is a penetration test report on a live system

cards.subject: STRIDE
says: is a checklist of six threat categories
covers spoofing, tampering and repudiation among them
cards.use: want a checklist to walk through each threat type for a component
not: is a scoring system for vulnerability severity

cards.subject: A trust boundary
says: is a point where data passes between different levels of trust
needs validation of whatever crosses it
cards.use: want to know where input must be validated as it crosses between components
not: is the edge of the company's physical premises

cards.subject: Broken access control
says: lets users act outside their permissions
is a major category of web application flaws
cards.use: find that a normal user can open an admin page by changing the URL
not: is a failure of encryption of data in transit

cards.subject: Insecure direct object reference
says: trusts an object id supplied by the client
lets one user read another user's record by changing the id
cards.use: see that changing an id in a request returns someone else's record
not: is an id that is too short to store

cards.subject: Elevation of privilege
says: lets an actor gain rights beyond those granted
is the E in STRIDE
cards.use: find that a basic user can make themselves an administrator
not: reads data the actor was never meant to see

cards.subject: Repudiation
says: lets an actor deny having performed an action
is answered by tamper-resistant audit logs
cards.use: need to prove who approved a change when they say they did not
not: alters data in transit without being noticed

cards.subject: GGLearn's password storage
says: keeps a salted scrypt hash and never the password itself
records the cost settings in a versioned format so they can be raised
cards.use: want to know how GGLearn stores sign-in passwords
not: encrypts passwords so administrators can recover them

cards.subject: GGLearn's session cookie
says: carries the user id, issued-at time, version and a message authentication code
lets the server detect tampering
cards.use: want to know what is inside GGLearn's signed session cookie
not: stores the user's password hash

cards.subject: GGLearn's session lifetime
says: is 30 days, enforced on the server from the signed issued-at time
does not depend on the cookie's maxAge
cards.use: need to explain why a client-controlled cookie expiry is not trusted by GGLearn
not: relies on the browser deleting the cookie after 30 days

cards.subject: GGLearn's session version
says: lets the server revoke all of a user's older sessions at once
is bumped by sign out everywhere and by offboarding
cards.use: want to log a user out of every device in GGLearn
not: extends every session by thirty days

cards.subject: GGLearn's dummy password check
says: runs a password verification even when the email is unknown
keeps response time from revealing which emails have accounts
cards.use: want to know why GGLearn verifies a password against a fixed hash for unknown emails
not: warms the hashing cache for the next real user

cards.subject: GGLearn's invite-only signup
says: lets people join only through an invitation link
closes the old route of open self-signup
cards.use: need to know how new people get an account in GGLearn
not: lets anyone on the internet create an account

cards.subject: GGLearn's per-request authorisation
says: re-reads the user's role from the database on every request
makes role changes and offboarding apply at once
cards.use: change someone's role in GGLearn and want to know when it takes effect
not: trusts the role stored in the session cookie until it expires

cards.subject: GGLearn's drill answer finding
says: shows a check returning the correct answer for any question id to any signed-in user
is fixed by keeping the answer key on the server and checking the caller's entitlement
cards.use: want the GGLearn example of broken access control
not: is an encryption error in the login cookie

cards.subject: GGLearn's login rate limiter
says: lives in process memory and resets on restart
suits a single PM2 process
cards.use: ask why GGLearn's login throttling would not work across several servers
not: is stored in a shared database table

cards.subject: GGLearn's client address handling
says: takes the client address a fixed number of hops from the end of X-Forwarded-For
uses the second-to-last entry behind Cloudflare and Apache
cards.use: need to know which X-Forwarded-For entry GGLearn trusts
not: uses the first entry because it is the original visitor

cards.subject: GGLearn's Cloudflare-only Apache rule
says: allows only Cloudflare's published address ranges
is generated by a script that refuses a list that looks wrong
cards.use: ask why visitors must not be able to reach Apache directly in GGLearn
not: is already active on the live virtual hosts by default

cards.subject: GGLearn's leaked-cookie response
says: bumps session versions or rotates the signing secret to sign everyone out
preserves logs while the cause is found
cards.use: suspect a signed GGLearn session has leaked and do not know whose
not: waits for each cookie to expire after 30 days

cards.subject: GG Social's rsync with the delete flag
says: removes server files that are absent from the source
destroys the production secrets file unless it is excluded
cards.use: are reminded how a deploy script could remove a server-only secrets file
not: uploads the server's secrets file back to the source

cards.subject: Losing GG Social's app secret
says: logs every user out
leaves stored platform tokens undecryptable
cards.use: want to know what breaks when the GG Social app secret is lost
not: only affects the colour theme of the site

cards.subject: GG Social's server-side secrets backup
says: is a copy of the secrets file kept on the server
allows a deleted file to be restored
cards.use: need to recover GG Social's deleted secrets file quickly
not: is stored in the repository next to the code

cards.subject: GG Money's deploy
says: never uploads the local config
keeps secrets out of what is shipped
cards.use: ask how GG Money keeps local settings from being shipped to the server
not: overwrites the server config with the local one each time
like: GG Social's rsync with the delete flag

cards.subject: GG Money's email key
says: is created with only the permission needed to send mail
avoids a full-access key that could read contacts and rewrite the account
cards.use: are told to create the GG Money email key and want to know why it is restricted
not: is a full-access key because it is simpler

cards.subject: The Moksy AI gateway's credential encryption
says: encrypts stored provider keys with AES-256-GCM using a master key from the environment
refuses to save credentials if the master key is not set
cards.use: want to know how the Moksy AI gateway protects stored provider keys
not: saves provider keys in plaintext when no master key is set

cards.subject: GG Money's forged account id finding
says: shows a forged account id reading another company's bank lines
is an insecure direct object reference
cards.use: want the GG Money example of trusting a client-supplied id
not: is a weak password hashing parameter

qa.q: What is the main purpose of multi-factor authentication?
qa.right: To make a stolen password alone insufficient to sign in
wrong: To make passwords unnecessary on every system
To speed up the sign-in process
To let several people share one account safely
qa.why: MFA adds a second, different kind of proof.

qa.q: Which is the safest way to handle an API key?
qa.right: Keep it in server-side configuration that is not committed to the repository
wrong: Paste it into the team chat so everyone has it
Hard-code it next to the feature that uses it
Email it to yourself as a backup
qa.why: Secrets belong outside source control and chat.

qa.q: What should you do first with an email that unexpectedly asks you to sign in through a link?
qa.right: Do not click; report it and go to the site by another route
wrong: Click the link to check whether it is genuine
Forward it to all colleagues as a warning
Reply and ask the sender to confirm by email
qa.why: Reporting and avoiding the link keeps the lure inert.

qa.q: Why do organisations keep software patched?
qa.right: Updates close known vulnerabilities that attackers exploit
wrong: Updates always add new features users want
Unpatched software cannot start
Patches make the network faster
qa.why: Patching removes known weaknesses.

qa.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?
qa.right: Authentication proves who you are; authorisation decides what you may do
wrong: Authentication decides what you may do; authorisation proves who you are
They are two names for the same check
Authentication happens only once a year
qa.why: Identity first, then permission.

qa.q: Why is a unique password per account recommended?
qa.right: One breached site then cannot unlock the others
wrong: Unique passwords never need to be changed
Sites reject duplicate passwords across accounts
Unique passwords cannot be phished
qa.why: Reuse is what makes credential stuffing work.

qa.q: Why should logs be copied to a separate system?
qa.right: An intruder on a host can delete the logs stored there
wrong: Separate systems compress logs better
Logs are only legal evidence if stored offsite in another country
Hosts cannot write logs and run applications at once
qa.why: Off-host copies preserve evidence.

qa.q: Which backup practice best protects against ransomware?
qa.right: Keep at least one copy that is immutable or offline, and test restores
wrong: Keep one backup on the file server for speed
Back up only once a year
Mount all backups permanently so they are easy to reach
qa.why: Ransomware tries to encrypt or delete reachable backups.

qa.q: What does the principle of least privilege mean?
qa.right: Give each account only the access its task needs
wrong: Give every manager full access to reduce requests
Grant access to everyone and remove it on complaint
Use one shared account to reduce the number of permissions
qa.why: Less access means less damage when compromised.

qa.q: What does a SIEM do?
qa.right: Collects logs from many sources and alerts when events match rules
wrong: Encrypts all network traffic
Scans code for typing errors
Blocks every unknown device from the network
qa.why: It centralises and correlates events.

qa.q: Why does a security awareness programme make reporting easy and blame-free?
qa.right: People who fear blame hide mistakes, and fast reports limit damage
wrong: Blame is illegal in most workplaces
Reports are only valid when anonymous
Easy reporting replaces the need for technical controls
qa.why: Early reports matter more than blame.

qa.q: What is full-disk encryption protecting against?
qa.right: Data being read from a lost or stolen device
wrong: Malware running on the device
Phishing emails reaching the user
Network eavesdropping on the office wifi
qa.why: It protects data at rest.

qa.q: Which statement about the cloud shared responsibility model is correct?
qa.right: The customer is responsible for configuring their own storage permissions and identities
wrong: The provider secures every customer configuration automatically
The customer secures the provider's data centres
Responsibility never changes whatever service is used
qa.why: Customers own their configuration and data.

qa.q: Which is the best reason to use a password manager?
qa.right: It lets you use a long, unique password for every account without remembering them
wrong: It makes every site support MFA
It removes the need for any second factor
It stops phishing pages from loading
qa.why: Unique strong passwords become practical.

qa.q: Which second factor is most resistant to a phishing page relaying the login?
qa.right: A hardware security key or passkey bound to the real site
wrong: An SMS code typed into the page
A password hint question
A six-digit code emailed to the user
qa.why: Origin-bound credentials will not respond to a look-alike domain.

qa.q: A scanner reports 400 findings. What is the sensible way to start?
qa.right: Prioritise by exposure, exploitability and asset value, not by score alone
wrong: Fix them in the order they appear in the report
Ignore anything below the highest severity band
Close the report until the next scan
qa.why: Context decides real risk.

qa.q: Why is a CVSS score alone not enough to decide what to patch first?
qa.right: It rates technical severity without knowing how exposed your system is
wrong: It only covers flaws older than a year
It is calculated randomly by the scanner
It measures the cost of the patch
qa.why: Environment and exploitation matter.

qa.q: Which describes an insecure direct object reference?
qa.right: A request id from the client is trusted without checking the caller owns the object
wrong: A database column with no index
A login page that is not served over TLS
A key that is too short to be secure
qa.why: The server must check ownership.

qa.q: Why is it risky to treat the first entry in X-Forwarded-For as the client address?
qa.right: The visitor can write that entry themselves
wrong: It is always the proxy's own address
Proxies remove it
It only holds IPv6 addresses
qa.why: Only entries added by your own proxies can be trusted.

qa.q: What is the purpose of a tabletop exercise?
qa.right: To rehearse the response to a simulated incident through discussion
wrong: To scan production for open ports
To restore a server from backup
To measure the speed of the network
qa.why: It tests plans without touching systems.

qa.q: What does a restore test prove that a successful backup job does not?
qa.right: That the data can actually be recovered and how long it takes
wrong: That the backup job is scheduled
That the backup is encrypted
That the backup is stored in the cloud
qa.why: Only a restore shows usability.

qa.q: What does network segmentation mainly achieve?
qa.right: It limits how far a breach in one zone can spread
wrong: It encrypts all traffic between users
It removes the need for patching
It makes every device share one address range
qa.why: Smaller blast radius.

qa.q: What is the correct order of the first stages of incident response?
qa.right: Prepare, detect and analyse, contain, eradicate, recover, review
wrong: Recover, contain, detect, review, prepare
Eradicate, announce, contain, detect
Detect, review, recover, contain
qa.why: The lifecycle follows this order.

qa.q: What is the best use of a phishing simulation?
qa.right: To measure reporting and give targeted coaching
wrong: To identify staff to discipline
To replace email filtering
To prove no one will ever click
qa.why: The goal is learning, not punishment.

qa.q: Which evidence best shows an auditor that quarterly access reviews took place?
qa.right: Dated review records showing who approved or removed which access
wrong: A statement from the manager that reviews happen
The policy document that says reviews are required
A screenshot of the login page
qa.why: Evidence must show the control operated.

qa.q: What does the recovery point objective of four hours mean?
qa.right: The business can tolerate losing up to four hours of data
wrong: Services must be restored within four hours
Backups are kept for four hours
Four people must approve every restore
qa.why: RPO is about data loss, RTO about downtime.

qa.q: Why is MFA fatigue effective against push approvals?
qa.right: The attacker repeats prompts until a tired user approves one
wrong: The push protocol has no encryption
The attacker guesses the six-digit code
The user's phone number is changed by the carrier
qa.why: It abuses human response, not cryptography.

qa.q: Why can a committed secret never be treated as safe after deleting the file?
qa.right: The value remains in history and clones, so it must be rotated
wrong: Deleted files are restored by the build server
Git encrypts history with the old key
It is safe once the branch is merged
qa.why: History keeps the value.

qa.q: What is the main benefit of short-lived credentials?
qa.right: A stolen token stops working soon without anyone acting
wrong: They never need to be issued
They are impossible to copy
They remove the need for authentication
qa.why: Expiry limits the window.

qa.q: What is a compensating control?
qa.right: A measure that reduces risk when the proper fix cannot yet be applied
wrong: A refund paid after a breach
A second copy of the vulnerable system
A promise to patch eventually
qa.why: It buys time while a fix is arranged.

qa.q: Why is an SOC 2 report not proof that a supplier cannot be breached?
qa.right: It reports on controls over a scope and period, not an absence of risk
wrong: It is only valid for U.S. suppliers
It is produced by the supplier without an auditor
It covers only physical security
qa.why: Assurance is not a guarantee.

qa.q: Why does envelope encryption help with key rotation?
qa.right: Only the small data keys must be re-wrapped when the master key changes
wrong: It makes the master key unnecessary
It encrypts the data twice at each rotation
It stores the master key beside the data
qa.why: Re-wrapping is cheaper than re-encrypting all data.

qa.q: Which design is most likely to survive a ransomware attack that obtains domain administrator rights?
qa.right: Immutable or offline backups that administrators cannot alter
wrong: Backups on a share the administrators manage
Snapshots stored on the same volume
A second copy on a mounted network drive
qa.why: The attacker can reach whatever the admin can.

qa.q: A new employee asks why they cannot have administrator rights on their laptop. Which answer is best?
qa.right: Everyday work does not need them, and removing them limits what malware can change
wrong: Administrator rights are only for senior staff
Laptops cannot have administrator accounts
It is a licensing restriction
qa.why: Least privilege on endpoints.

qa.q: A developer realises they pushed an API key to a shared repository an hour ago. What should they do first?
qa.right: Rotate the key, then clean up and review its use
wrong: Delete the file in a new commit and move on
Wait to see whether anyone notices
Ask everyone to stop pulling the repository
qa.why: The key must be treated as compromised.

qa.q: A team receives an email from the apparent finance director asking for urgent change of supplier bank details. What is the right response?
qa.right: Verify through a known separate channel before acting
wrong: Reply asking for confirmation by email
Change the details because the sender is senior
Forward it to the supplier
qa.why: Out-of-band verification defeats business email compromise.

qa.q: A user reports their laptop was stolen from a car. What should the response include?
qa.right: Revoke sessions, trigger a remote wipe and check the disk was encrypted
wrong: Wait a week in case it is returned
Change only the wifi password
Reimage the laptop remotely and skip the report
qa.why: Limit exposure quickly and confirm the data was protected.

qa.q: An analyst sees hundreds of alerts a day and starts closing them unread. What is the best fix?
qa.right: Tune or remove noisy rules so alerts are worth reading
wrong: Add more alert rules of every type
Turn off all alerts after hours
Ask the analyst to read faster
qa.why: Alert fatigue is a design problem.

qa.q: A supplier will process customer data for your company. What should happen before access is granted?
qa.right: Assess its security and agree what data and access it gets
wrong: Sign the contract and assess later
Give it administrator access to speed onboarding
Accept its own statement of compliance without review
qa.why: Vendor risk starts before onboarding.

qa.q: Staff report a stranger following them through the badge door. What is the best response?
qa.right: Politely ask them to badge in or report to security
wrong: Hold the door for them
Ignore it as the stranger looks professional
Disable the badge readers for the day
qa.why: Tailgating bypasses the badge control.

qa.q: After a breach is contained, a manager wants to restore service right away. What should you check first?
qa.right: That the cause is removed and the restored systems are known-good
wrong: That the press release is approved
That the logs are deleted
That every user has changed their password to the same value
qa.why: Restoring before eradication risks reinfection.

qa.q: A critical internal flaw scores higher than an exposed one, but the exposed one has a public exploit. Which first?
qa.right: The exposed flaw with a public exploit
wrong: The higher score regardless of exposure
Neither until the next scan
Whichever is older
qa.why: Exploitability and exposure drive risk.

qa.q: A legacy system cannot be patched until next quarter. What is a reasonable step now?
qa.right: Isolate it behind segmentation and restrict who can reach it
wrong: Remove it from the vulnerability scan
Leave it exposed and note the date
Disable logging to save space
qa.why: Compensating controls reduce exposure while waiting.

qa.q: Two engineers share one administrator account. What is the main problem for investigations?
qa.right: Actions cannot be traced to a person
wrong: The account will expire sooner
Passwords cannot be hashed
Sessions are no longer encrypted
qa.why: Individual accountability needs individual accounts.

qa.q: After an employee leaves, you find their account still active in three systems. Which control failed?
qa.right: The leaver process and access reviews
wrong: Network segmentation
Full-disk encryption
TLS certificate renewal
qa.why: Offboarding must reach every system.

qa.q: A storage bucket holding customer files is found public. What is the best first move?
qa.right: Close public access, preserve logs and check what was accessed
wrong: Delete the bucket to remove the problem
Wait until the monthly review
Move it to another region
qa.why: Contain, keep evidence, then assess impact.

qa.q: A single sign-on outage locks out every administrator. What should have been prepared?
qa.right: A sealed, monitored break-glass account
wrong: A shared admin password in a chat channel
A permanent bypass of MFA for all admins
A larger password policy
qa.why: Emergency access needs controls too.

qa.q: An attacker has captured a session after the user completed MFA through a proxy page. Which control would have prevented it?
qa.right: Passkeys or hardware keys bound to the real site
wrong: A longer password
More frequent password changes
Blocking SMS codes only
qa.why: Origin-bound credentials will not sign for the proxy.

qa.q: Your detection finds an admin account signing in from two continents within minutes. What is the best first move?
qa.right: Contain by revoking sessions and resetting the credential, keeping evidence
wrong: Ignore it as a VPN error
Delete the account's logs
Wait for the user to report it
qa.why: Contain first and preserve evidence.

qa.q: Which company practice fits GGLearn's handling of passwords?
qa.right: Store only a salted scrypt hash in a versioned format
wrong: Store encrypted passwords for password recovery
Store passwords in plaintext in a protected table
Store an unsalted fast hash
qa.why: The company design keeps only salted, versioned hashes.

qa.q: In GGLearn, why does the server enforce the 30-day session lifetime itself?
qa.right: Because the cookie's maxAge is controlled by the client
wrong: Because browsers ignore all cookies after a day
Because the cookie cannot hold a date
Because 30 days is a legal requirement
qa.why: The signed issued-at time is trusted instead.

qa.q: A GGLearn user is offboarded. Why do their existing sessions stop working at once?
qa.right: Authorisation is re-read from the database on each request
wrong: The session cookie deletes itself
The browser clears cookies at midnight
The rate limiter blocks them
qa.why: Status and role are checked every request.

qa.q: What is the reason GGLearn runs a dummy password check for unknown emails?
qa.right: So response time does not reveal which emails have accounts
wrong: To cache hashes for the next user
To log failed attempts
Because the library needs one call per request
qa.why: Uniform timing prevents enumeration.

qa.q: The GGLearn login limiter keeps its counters in memory. What does that imply?
qa.right: It resets on restart and fits only a single process
wrong: It shares counts across every server
It survives restarts
It cannot rate limit by address
qa.why: In-memory state is local to the process.

qa.q: A GG Social deploy used rsync with the delete flag and the secrets file vanished. What follows if the app secret was lost?
qa.right: Everyone is logged out and stored platform tokens cannot be decrypted
wrong: Only the theme changes
Nothing, the secret regenerates identically
Only new users are affected
qa.why: Restore the file from the server-side backup.

qa.q: Why does the Moksy AI gateway refuse to save credentials when its master key is not set?
qa.right: Failing closed is safer than silently saving plaintext
wrong: The database needs a key to open
Providers require a key to be set first
The cipher cannot handle empty keys
qa.why: A missing protection should stop the operation.

qa.q: A suspected GGLearn session leak has no known victim. What is the most direct lever?
qa.right: Rotate the signing secret or bump session versions to sign everyone out
wrong: Ask users to clear their cookies
Wait for 30-day expiry
Disable the login rate limiter
qa.why: Signed cookies and a version give clear revocation levers.

qa.q: The Cloudflare-only Apache rule exists in the repository but the live vhosts do not include it. What is the consequence?
qa.right: Visitors can still reach Apache directly and spoof X-Forwarded-For
wrong: It already blocks all non-Cloudflare traffic
Cloudflare traffic is blocked
The rate limiter is disabled
qa.why: The rule takes effect only once included.
